title: Interview · Behavioral (STAR)
description: Eight behavioral competencies from the JD, each paired with the transferable STAR-answer structure and my own real story to tell — including the two honestly-flagged gaps.

cards.front: Tell me about a time you drove adoption of a new engineering practice or tool on your team.
cards.general: This probes whether you can change how a team works, not just how you personally work — influence without needing formal authority. Structure it as STAR: the Situation (a team not yet using the practice), the Task (why adoption mattered), the Action (what you concretely did to bring others along — not just that you used the tool yourself but that you set norms, coached, and lowered the barrier for teammates), and the Result. Name the practice specifically, describe the informal norms you established, and show judgment about responsible use — where the practice needs guardrails or verification. Quantify or characterize the change in the team's workflow where you can.
cards.specific: My story: I drove daily-workflow adoption of Cursor / Claude Opus / Copilot at USAA, and I set informal review norms with teammates on when to trust AI-generated code versus verify it line by line. The responsible-AI coaching half — deciding when to trust versus check generated code — is what makes this a leadership story and not just a personal-productivity anecdote. This is the AI-assisted-engineering competency named in some form on all 8 reqs.
cards.hint: Rehearse this one first, word for word — it's named on every one of the 8 reqs and is the single highest-probability behavioral question across the board.

cards.front: Tell me about a risky migration or a piece of critical infrastructure you owned.
cards.general: This probes ownership under risk: can you take responsibility for something whose failure has real consequences, and did you drive the key technical decisions rather than just execute someone else's plan. Structure with STAR and make sure you own the decision — especially the design choices where you set direction. Explain what made it risky (blast radius, migration from a legacy system, no easy rollback), the architectural decisions you owned, and how you de-risked it. End on a concrete result.
cards.specific: My story: the monolith → event-driven notification rebuild at USAA. I was the principal developer and I owned the service-boundary design — the core architectural decision that defined how the rebuilt platform was split into independently scalable stages. I emphasize my ownership of the boundaries, not just participation in the migration.

cards.front: Tell me about a time you delivered a GenAI or agentic system for a client or stakeholder — from proposal through to production.
cards.general: This is the client-facing GenAI/agentic delivery competency (sharpest on Senior Lead AI, PublicCloud roles). It probes end-to-end delivery for someone other than yourself: shaping the proposal, navigating stakeholders, and actually landing it in production — not just prototyping. Structure with STAR and stress the proposal-to-production arc: how you scoped it, what you built, and that it shipped. Show you can translate a stakeholder need into a delivered, grounded system.
cards.specific: My story: FrostByte, the Snowflake MCP server — I proposed it, built it, and it was adopted by the team as a running tool for AI-assisted analytics, and Project Overview, my VS Code walkthrough extension, covers the same proposal-through-adoption arc for a different stakeholder need (developer onboarding rather than data analytics). These are my two internally adopted, client-facing GenAI/agentic deliveries, and I don't reach beyond them for this story.

cards.front: Tell me about something significant you built end-to-end, largely on your own.
cards.general: This probes breadth and independent ownership — can you carry a system across every layer (design, backend, frontend, deployment) without a team to lean on. Structure with STAR and let the scope speak: name the layers you personally owned and point to something concrete and verifiable as the result. Independent, full-stack delivery is the signal here.
cards.specific: My story: LocalLLM — a full-stack solo build I did myself, with a public repo and a live Hugging Face Space demo. The public repo plus live demo is the verifiable result that makes my 'built it all myself' claim credible — I lead with the fact that it's demonstrable.

cards.front: Tell me about a time you owned infrastructure that multiple teams depended on.
cards.general: This is the cross-team infra-ownership competency (sharpest on VP-FullStack, DigitalAuth). It probes responsibility for shared infrastructure — where your decisions affect other teams' reliability — and your depth in the underlying platform. Structure with STAR, name the specific platforms, and be ready for a technical follow-up on the trade-offs of the tooling you chose. Show you understand the operational implications for the teams downstream of you.
cards.specific: My story: container orchestration on OpenShift + Kubernetes. I pair this with the Kubernetes-vs-OpenShift drill in 07-distributed-systems-and-observability.md so I'm ready for the technical follow-up on why OpenShift over vanilla Kubernetes.
cards.hint: Have the Kubernetes-vs-OpenShift technical drill (07-distributed-systems-and-observability.md) loaded for the follow-up.

cards.front: Tell me about a technical disagreement or a hard trade-off you had to make.
cards.general: This probes technical judgment and how you handle differing views: can you reason about a real trade-off, commit to a decision, and articulate why. Structure with STAR and own the decision — state the two options, the trade-off between them, the criteria you weighed, and the choice you made and stand behind. Avoid framing it as conflict for its own sake; the signal is disciplined reasoning under a genuine trade-off.
cards.specific: My story: the synchronous-acknowledgment vs. asynchronous-processing decoupling decision at USAA — the architectural choice behind the notification platform's front-door design. The trade-off is returning an immediate sync ack to the caller versus decoupling the heavy work asynchronously behind a queue; I can explain why the front door acks fast and hands downstream work off async.

cards.front: Tell me about a time you mentored someone or showed leadership without holding a formal leadership title.
cards.general: This probes influence and leadership independent of a title (sharpest on Lead ai-ml and Senior Lead AI). The strongest answers are specific: a named person whose approach changed because of you, a decision someone came to you for, or a design trade-off you walked someone through live and in real time — not just 'people used a tool I made.' Structure with STAR around one concrete before/after.
cards.specific: OPEN GAP — I don't yet have a single strong story here. I will NOT fabricate one. The pivot language for handling this live is in 08-mandatory-drills-and-weak-claims.md; the raw material I'm mining is my code-review ownership at USAA, the Project Overview onboarding tool, and my Ironhack peer tutoring. I should keep mining for a sharper single example before any HM round, using these prompts: Did any teammate specifically change their workflow because of my code-review comments — a before/after I can name? Did anyone ask me directly for guidance on a specific technical decision (not just 'used my tool')? Is there a moment I walked someone through a design trade-off in real time, live, not via a tool?
cards.hint: Flagged gap — use the pivot language from 08-mandatory-drills-and-weak-claims.md and keep mining for a sharper single example before any HM round.

cards.front: Tell me about a failure or a mistake, and what you learned from it.
cards.general: This appears in essentially all HM/behavioral rounds. It probes self-awareness and growth: a real, owned mistake with a clear 'what I'd do differently.' Structure with STAR, pick the smallest honest example that has a genuine lesson, take real ownership without over-dramatizing, and land on the concrete change you made afterward. A small, real failure story beats an invented large one.
cards.specific: OPEN GAP — I don't yet have a covering story here. I will NOT invent one. Before the first screen I should mine for a misjudged estimate, a production incident, or a design decision I'd reverse, from USAA or EnergyBot. My mining prompts: Has any stage of the notification pipeline ever needed a hotfix or rollback I was involved in? Was there a chunking/embedding choice on FedInsight that I had to redo after it didn't work as expected? Did any EnergyBot forecasting model I worked on need retraining or rework after a validation surprise? I should pick the smallest honest example with a clear 'what I'd do differently' — a small, real failure story beats an invented large one.
cards.hint: Flagged gap — mine a real, small example (USAA or EnergyBot) before the first screen; never invent a failure.
